title: Why calibration?
content:
Why do I need to do the calibration?


The calibration process is essential for personalizing the app’s feedback and exercises to your specific needs. Everyone’s body and muscle activity levels are different, and by recording your baseline muscle activity, we can ensure that the exercises you follow are tailored specifically to you.


Here’s why it matters:

Personalization: Each person has a unique level of muscle activation, both at rest and during exertion. Calibration helps us understand your specific muscle behaviour so we can adjust the difficulty and intensity of exercises just for you.

Normalizing Data: The calibration process records your baseline muscle activity and then uses this data to normalize all your future exercise measurements. This ensures that the targets and goals we set are achievable based on your muscle capacity rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

Safety: Proper calibration ensures that exercises are challenging yet safe, keeping you within healthy activation ranges for your back and core muscles without overexerting or underworking.


By completing the calibration, you are setting the foundation for a more effective, personalized, and safe workout routine that suits your body’s specific needs.


The calibration procedure takes 3 steps:

Step 1 will record your baseline muscle activity when you are at rest. It helps personalize your exercises later by understanding your natural resting posture.

Step 2 increases your back muscle activity and helps determine the minimum level of engagement your back muscles should reach during exercises.

Step 3 helps measure your abdominal muscle activity under slight pressure, which will be used to guide you in activating your abdominal core during exercises.

title: Exercising
content:
How to tell if you’re exercising at the right level

This guide can help you to understand if you’re exercising at the right level. It’ll also let you see how much pain or discomfort is acceptable.

It can be helpful to rate your pain out of 10 (0 being no pain 10 being the worst pain you have ever had), for example:

0 to 3 – minimal pain

4 to 5 – acceptable pain

6 to 10 – excessive pain


Pain during exercise

Aim to keep your pain within a rating of 0 to 5. If your pain gets above this level, you can change the exercises by:

reducing the number of times you do a movement

reducing the speed of a movement

increasing rest time between movements


Pain after exercise

Exercise should not make your existing back pain worse overall. However, practicing new exercises can sometimes cause short term muscle pain as the body gets used to moving in new ways. This kind of pain should ease quickly and your pain should be no worse the morning after you’ve exercised.
